results.summary: This project implements three selectable minigames that take button input and display output on a 7-segment display. The design is written in Verilog and runs at 10 MHz. Testing is done by pressing different buttons to play the games. External hardware required includes eight buttons and a 7-segment display.

This is a Nauta operational transconductance amplifier (OTA) with 2-bit digital trimming for tuning. It is an analog design implemented at the transistor level, based on the Nauta OTA circuit with digital trim as described in referenced literature. The design requires differential AC input signals and provides differential outputs, with digital trimming controlled via digital pins. External test equipment is needed to provide inputs and observe outputs, but no special hardware is required.

Sleepy Chip is a dual-mode digital audio synthesizer featuring a 3-waveform oscillator with streaming capability and a delta-sigma DAC output. It supports both traditional synthesis (oscillator plus waveform mixing) and direct sample streaming. The design is controlled via SPI and includes a gate input, hardware reset, and outputs for DAC, gate LED, oscillator run, and sync. It is implemented in SystemVerilog and fits in a 1x1 Tiny Tapeout tile.

This is an 8-bit arithmetic logic unit (ALU) that performs arithmetic and bitwise operations on integer binary numbers. It uses a state machine to read two 8-bit inputs (A and B) via the 8 digital input pins, with operation control and status output over the bidirectional pins. The design is implemented in Verilog and runs at 50 MHz. Testing instructions are not provided (marked as TODO), so the exact usage is unclear.

This project is a hardcoded squarewave synthesizer sequencer that plays a specific musical progression. It provides tempo control via two input pins (tempo up and tempo down) and outputs a squarewave signal to a speaker. The design is written in VHDL and requires a 4.8 MHz clock and an external speaker to play the music. It is a simple plug-and-play design with minimal documentation.

This is a time-domain comparator-based analog-to-digital converter (ADC). It has analog inputs for differential signals (VIN, VIP) and a common-mode voltage (VCM), and provides a 9-bit digital output (DATA[8:0]) along with a clock output (CKO). The design is implemented in an analog/mixed-signal style and occupies a 2x2 tile area. No documentation is provided beyond the pin names and one-line description, so details of operation and testing are not available.

This project is an attempt to characterize the SKY130 technology and perform aging experiments. The design is written in VHDL but all pins are marked as unused, and the documentation states that details will be updated later. There is no information on how the design works or how to test it. External hardware is not specified.

This project implements an LED spinner game on a 7-segment display, resembling a roulette wheel. The wheel spins at a speed set by four input pins, and the user can guess the stopping position using six bidirectional pins; a correct guess lights up the decimal point. It uses a linear feedback shift register (LFSR) to generate pseudo-random stopping positions and includes a stop input to halt the wheel. The design is written in Verilog and requires external hardware such as DIP switches and a 7-segment display for testing.

This is a 4-bit ALU with an integrated 8x4-bit register file. It supports arithmetic and logical operations, as well as register-file read/write access, with opcodes selected via four bidirectional pins. The 8-bit output contains a 4-bit result and four flags (zero, sign, overflow, carry). The design is implemented in Verilog and requires no external hardware, though DIP switches and LEDs are suggested for demonstration.

This is a tiny hardware authentication engine that generates a 4-digit one-time password (OTP) using a 16-bit linear feedback shift register (LFSR) with time-bound validity and multi-attempt lockout. It uses a finite state machine to control authentication, retry, and timeout operations, and displays results on seven-segment displays. The design is implemented in Verilog and requires external hardware such as seven-segment displays, push buttons, and a clock for testing. It is lightweight and Tiny Tapeout friendly, with observable outputs on FPGA.
